summary: Gives guidance to people who want to use DHCPv6 in their IPv6 deployments, and in particular discusses how to provide semi-redundant DHCPv6 services. It is a Best Current Practice.

eli5.summary: If the person who hands out name tags is away, a second person can step in. This explains how to set up a backup helper for the job.

questions: what is the dhcpv6 preference option
dhcpv6 split prefix vs identical prefix
is there a dhcpv6 failover protocol
subtitle: How to run two or more DHCPv6 servers for the same clients when no standard failover protocol exists.

tldr.problem: Operators want redundant DHCPv6 service, but there is no standards-based failover protocol, so servers cannot share lease state.
tldr.mechanism: Run at least two independent servers and use the DHCPv6 preference option plus one of three prefix layouts (split, multiple unique, or identical) to steer clients and keep pools from clashing.
tldr.outcome: The result is only semi-redundant service: servers do not exchange leases, so failures can still strand bindings, leave stale DNS records and hide behind identical configurations.

facts.label: Server-to-server lease sync
facts.value: Not possible until a failover protocol exists

today: RFC 6853 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 180) and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes an interim approach and states that complete redundancy has to wait for a standardized DHCPv6 failover protocol.

sections.title: Why Semi-Redundant DHCPv6
sections.content:
Redundancy and high availability for IPv6 infrastructure are desirable and, in some deployments, mandatory. For DHCPv6, though, there is no standards-based failover or redundancy protocol.

RFC 6853 therefore describes an interim architecture for semi-redundant services built from existing protocols. It says plainly that complete redundancy will not be available until a DHCPv6 failover protocol is standardized, and it points to a separate requirements document for such a protocol.
sections.eli5: There is no official way yet for two DHCPv6 servers to cover for each other. This document shows a workable stand-in until there is one.

sections.title: Scope and Assumptions
sections.content:
Two environments are discussed: service provider and enterprise. In both, at least two DHCPv6 servers serve the same clients and do not directly communicate with each other when assigning addresses or configuration. Clients run stateful DHCPv6 to get at least one IPv6 address, and they must handle the preference option and process ADVERTISE messages as RFC 3315 requires.

In the service provider case the clients are customer premises equipment such as cable modems and home routers, which may also use prefix delegation or stateless DHCPv6. In the enterprise case the clients are end hosts such as desktops, laptops and printers that typically do not need a delegated prefix, and relay agents only act as a transport.

Applying the same approaches to prefix delegation is called theoretical and was not investigated thoroughly. One drawback it names is that a split prefix model doubles the use of resources.
sections.eli5: The setup is for places with at least two helper servers that work on their own, such as an internet provider or an office network.

sections.title: What Servers, Relays and Clients Must Do
sections.content:
Servers must be RFC 3315 compliant. Support for stateful DHCPv6 and the preference option is essential. Where needed they must also support prefix delegation (RFC 3633) and stateless DHCPv6 (RFC 3736).

Relay agents must be RFC 3315 compliant and must be able to relay DHCPv6 messages to more than one destination.

Clients must be RFC 3315 compliant, must acquire at least one address with stateful DHCPv6, and must recognize and follow the preference option servers send. Prefix delegation is required only if the deployment needs it, and stateless DHCPv6 is optional.
sections.eli5: Everyone has to follow the normal DHCPv6 rules. Messages must reach more than one server, and the client must listen when a server says how much it wants to be picked.

sections.title: Three Deployment Models
sections.content:
The servers are used as they are, with no inter-server communication. The solution does not affect DHCPv4. The examples use /64 prefixes, but other lengths may be used. The preference option decides which server wins: an ADVERTISE with preference 255 tells the client to send a REQUEST to that server immediately, while a lower value or no preference option makes the client wait for further ADVERTISE messages.

Split prefixes

Each server gets a unique, non-overlapping pool carved from one /64. The RFC's example splits 2001:db8:1:1::/64 into two /65 pools. Both servers are active at once. Bindings can become unevenly spread over time, and if a server fails, rebinding to the other will ultimately fail because it has a different pool, so the client gets a new binding. Shorter T1, T2, valid and preferred lifetimes reduce disruption but add load on the servers. Separate pools also make failures easier to spot.

Multiple unique prefixes

Each server has its own non-overlapping prefix, and a /64 pool equal to it. The prefixes need not be adjacent, and split prefixes are a special case of this model. The network must be configured with several prefixes on the client-facing interfaces. The model drastically increases prefix consumption, brings operational challenges, and offers no clean migration path to a future failover protocol.

Identical prefixes

Every server has the same prefix and pool, and only the preference differs. This places no extra addressing demands on the network and may ease migration to a future failover protocol. It gives no help with dynamic DNS updates or leasequery, and failures are less obvious.
sections.eli5: You can give each helper a different pile of tags, a different table to sit at, or the very same pile. Each choice has its own good and bad sides.

sections.title: Challenges and Issues
sections.content:
Because the servers do not talk to each other, three problems stand out.

  • Identical prefixes: both servers must use the same allocation algorithm and policy, otherwise they may give the same address to two clients. Relays are expected to forward client messages to all servers. The client names its chosen server by its DUID in the Server-ID option, and the other server discards the request.
  • Dynamic DNS: if server A assigns a lease and adds an AAAA record, and server B later assigns a different lease when A is down, two AAAA records exist with no sign of which is active. If A never recovers, its record may never be removed. The DHCID record (RFC 4701) and conflict resolution (RFC 4703) help but do not cover every case.
  • Leasequery: lease data from RFC 5007 or RFC 5460 is unavailable while the granting server is down, until it returns with its data restored or the client renews against another server.

Exchanging or synchronizing leases between servers is not possible until a failover protocol is standardized or proprietary solutions become available.
sections.eli5: Because the helpers never compare notes, they might hand out the same tag twice, or leave old notes lying around. Using the same rules on both helps avoid mix-ups.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The interim architecture adds concerns beyond those in Section 23 of RFC 3315. Dynamic DNS updates under these models may leave abandoned DNS records even with the conflict resolution of RFC 4703. The RFC says this is no worse than a single server crashing and losing its lease database.

With identical prefixes, all servers must use the same allocation procedure and policy. Otherwise the same lease may be assigned to two clients. In some cases this can be recovered using Duplicate Address Detection and the DHCPv6 DECLINE mechanism.
sections.eli5: The main risk is two kids getting the same name tag. Using the same rules on both servers prevents that, and a kid can say no to a duplicate.

Different prefix and /64 pool on each server
Drastic prefix consumption; no clean migration path
Same prefix and pool on every server
